The Wood River sculpin (Cottus leiopomus) is a small, benthic freshwater fish endemic to the Wood River system in central Idaho. Studies of its life history have revealed that females attain an ultimate total length of 12.1 cm [Li = 12.1 cm], while males reach a comparable maximum size of 12.1 cm [Li = 12.1 cm], indicating minimal sexual dimorphism in overall body length for this species. This modest size is typical of many cottid fishes adapted to cool, fast-flowing stream habitats. Analyses of growth trajectories and gonadal development indicate that the total length at puberty for females is approximately 5.5 cm [Lp = approximately 5.5 cm], whereas males begin maturing at a slightly larger size, around 6 cm [Lp = around 6 cm]. This slight delay in male maturation is a pattern observed in several other members of the genus Cottus and is often linked to the energetic demands of establishing and defending nesting territories during the spawning season.

At the onset of exogenous feeding, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of this species possess a wet weight at birth of 0.0023 g [Wwb = 0.0023 g], a value derived from the diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs. This extremely small initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva and places a premium on the rapid development of feeding structures. As individuals grow and approach the pubertal transition, female Wood River sculpin typically attain a wet weight at puberty of 2.2 g [Wwp = 2.2 g]. Males, in contrast, reach the same developmental milestone at a heavier body condition, with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 2.89 g [Wwp = 2.89 g]. This difference in mass at maturity likely reflects the greater somatic investment required by males to achieve the body size necessary for successful competition over spawning sites beneath large cobbles.

Adults of the species go on to achieve an ultimate wet weight that is substantially greater than their mass at puberty. For both sexes, the ultimate wet weight for females is 24.9 g [Wwi = 24.9 g], and the ultimate wet weight for males is likewise 24.9 g [Wwi = 24.9 g]. This convergence in asymptotic body mass between sexes is noteworthy given the divergence observed at maturation, suggesting that after puberty, growth trajectories converge under similar resource limitations. The pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that once the primary reproductive roles are established, the energetic scope for additional somatic growth becomes constrained by the local prey base of aquatic insect larvae and benthic invertebrates. Field surveys of adult populations in the Big Wood River and its tributaries have confirmed that very few individuals exceed this mass, supporting the idea that it represents a genuine upper limit under prevailing environmental conditions.

The longevity of Wood River sculpin has been estimated from both otolith annuli and recapture data from a long-term mark-recapture study. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 2,920 d [am = 2,920 d] under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This lifespan of approximately eight years is relatively extended for a fish of such small body size and is likely linked to the cold thermal regime of its native habitat, which slows metabolic rates and cellular senescence. In the wild, where temperatures fluctuate seasonally and predation pressure from larger salmonids such as rainbow trout is present, the realized lifespan may be shorter, but the inherent physiological potential appears to be set by these cool-water conditions. The slow pace of life implied by this combination of small adult mass and long maximum lifespan places Cottus leiopomus at the slow end of the life-history continuum among North American freshwater cottids.

Reproductive ecology in this species is characterized by a single, annual spawning event that occurs in late winter or early spring. Females deposit their eggs in a single clutch per year, adhering them to the underside of a flat rock within a nest guarded by a male. The fecundity per clutch is tightly linked to female body size, with gravid females producing up to 200 eggs per clutch in a single spawning event. Following fertilization, the eggs incubate for an extended period, during which the male fans the clutch and defends against egg predators. Upon hatching, the prolarvae remain within the gravel interstitial spaces, absorbing their yolk sacs before emerging as free-swimming larvae. This parental care behavior is energetically costly for the guarding male, who may lose substantial body mass over the incubation period, and it represents a key constraint on the species' overall reproductive output within a given season.
